21.text: Every Lunar New Year my mother steams a whole fish and nobody may flip it over — flipping capsizes the family boat. Superstition, sure, but I'd defend it in court.
Sunday calls with my grandmother in Lagos. Rain or shine, 4pm her time, and she always asks whether I've eaten before anything else.
We write one wish on paper and burn it in the garden on New Year's Eve. My father started it after the war and never once explained why.
Birthday person picks dinner, no vetoes. At nine I made everyone eat instant noodles with cheese slices, and they honored it with straight faces.
Making tamales in December, assembly line style. The aunts arguing over masa consistency is the actual tradition, if we're honest.
First snow of the year, everyone goes outside no matter the hour. My mother did it as a girl in Warsaw. Last year we stood in pajamas at 2am.
The tablecloth everyone signs at Christmas, which my aunt then embroiders over. Forty years of handwriting on it now, including people who are gone.
Eid mornings my father wakes the house with the same off-key song he's sung since before I was born. I would pay to keep hearing it forever.
My grandfather's toast before big meals: he raises his glass and says nothing, just looks at each of us in turn. The silence says more than any speech.
Every road trip starts with the same petrol station meat pie, even now that we could afford better. Some rituals are about the badness.
Mooncakes split sixteen ways so everyone gets a sliver, even the baby. My grandmother insists that a whole one to yourself is loneliness.
We visit my great-grandmother's grave each spring and tell her the year's news out loud, gossip included. She would have hated being left out.
The Boxing Day leftovers sandwich contest, judged harshly by my mum. There is a trophy. It's a gravy boat spray-painted gold.
Reading the same tattered Tintin aloud on the first night of every holiday, doing all the voices. My kids are teenagers and still demand it.
Friday dinner debates. My father posts the week's question on the fridge every Monday so we all have time to prepare our arguments.
Picking olives at my uncle's grove each October. Everyone complains for the entire weekend and then talks about it lovingly all year.

23.text: 'Country Roads', but the version everyone at my village karaoke bar sings, half in Japanese. Home is wherever that comes on.
Teresa Teng's 'The Moon Represents My Heart'. My mother hummed it while doing dishes; now I hum it doing mine in Toronto.
Honestly, the call to prayer at dusk in Karachi. It meant everyone heading home for dinner at once. I still stop walking when I hear one.
The ice cream truck jingle from my street in Melbourne — Greensleeves at triple speed. One bar of it and I'm eight, sprinting for coins.
'Waka Waka'. Not deep, but it was the 2010 World Cup and my whole street in Bogota danced for a month. Home is that particular summer.
My dad's old Fairuz cassette that lived in the car. Every school run began with her voice and his genuinely terrible harmonies.
Whatever my upstairs neighbor was practicing on accordion in Kyiv. Badly, at 7am, for years. I miss it more than I ever thought possible.
The rice cooker's little completion melody. That tune meant dinner in ten minutes and my grandmother yelling at us to wash our hands.
'Ne me quitte pas'. My parents danced to it in the kitchen when they thought we were asleep. We weren't. We watched from the stairs.
The church bells in my grandmother's town in Galicia rang slightly flat. Perfectly tuned bells sound wrong to me now, like a stranger's house.
The Sunday cricket commentary theme on the radio. Not quite a song, but it meant my father was home and the whole flat would smell of curry soon.
'Yeh Dosti', sung with my brother on one bicycle — me on the handlebars, both of us convinced we could actually sing. We could not.
'The Wellerman'. My kids played it nonstop during lockdown, so home is now the three of us stomping around the kitchen like sailors.
My mother's off-key lullaby that exists nowhere but her voice — a tune her own mother improvised in a refugee camp. Three generations carry it now.
The intro music to the 8pm news. Sounds silly, but it meant the whole family on one sofa, and the world briefly made sense from there.
Rain on a tin roof in Kerala. My grandfather called it the house singing. No recorded song has ever come close to it.

25.text: Left a stable government job at 41 to open a bakery. Everyone said I was mad. I was, slightly. The bread turned out good, though.
Boarded a plane alone at nineteen with one suitcase and my grandmother's ring, moving to a country where I knew nobody and not one word.
Told my father I wasn't taking over the family shop. Hardest sentence of my life, delivered over tea that had gone completely cold.
Sang at my sister's wedding despite the stutter I'd hidden for twenty years. My voice shook for one verse, and then it simply didn't.
Jumped into an Amsterdam canal after a stranger's dog. The dog swam out fine on its own. I did not. It still counts.
Asked my now-husband to dance when he was clearly out of my league. He claims he was about to ask me. He is a liar and I love him.
Called an ambulance for myself when everything in me wanted to insist I was fine. Small, quiet, and it saved my life.
Reported my boss for stealing wages from the kitchen staff. Lost that job, kept every single friend I made there.
Learned to swim at seventy. My granddaughter taught me in the shallow end, and I cried the first time I floated without her hands under me.
Ate my mother-in-law's fermented shark at my first dinner with the family and kept a straight face. She still tells this story with pride.
Stood up before two hundred parents at the school meeting and said, in my broken Danish, that my son was being bullied. My hands shook throughout.
Divorced at 55 in a family where nobody divorces. My mother didn't speak to me for a year. Then one day she rang and said she was proud.
Went back to finish secondary school at 34, sitting exams beside kids my son's age. They called me auntie. I passed everything.
At fifteen I confessed I'd been copying my best friend's homework for a year and once let her take the blame. Terrifying. She forgave me by lunch.
Held my grandfather's hand while they turned the machines off, because everyone else had left the room and someone had to stay.
Drove through my first Lagos roundabout at rush hour. Some people summit mountains; I merged. Same energy, I promise you.

27.text: Jollof rice, my mother's method, party quantity. And yes, I will fight the Ghanaian side of the family before the pot even boils.
Dumplings, because nobody is allowed to just watch. Youngest to oldest, everyone folds, and we mock whoever's come out like sad little hats.
Pancakes at midnight, whatever the actual time is. My kids believe breakfast tastes better when it's technically wrong, and they're right.
My late father's lentil soup, from the recipe he never wrote down. I have almost cracked it. Twenty years of almost.
Bigos, my grandmother's way, which takes three days. So really I'd be cooking us three days together. That is the entire point of the dish.
A full English at 7am sharp with proper tea, and I will not be taking questions about the baked beans from the Americans present.
Khichdi with far too much ghee. It's what my grandmother made after every long journey. You are not home until you've eaten it.
Ceviche, if I can find real limes, made at the counter so everyone hovers and steals pieces before it is technically ready.
Nothing fancy: rice, fried eggs with crispy edges, soy sauce, sixteen spoons. The dish of every tired evening of my childhood.
Injera, started the night before, so the batter is bubbling when everyone wakes. The smell alone would pull the whole house downstairs.
Pavlova first, dinner later. Life is uncertain and my aunt's rule was dessert priority. She lived to ninety-six on that policy.
Pho from scratch, and I'd make the teenagers watch the broth for six hours. Patience is the actual family recipe being passed down.
Fresh pasta with the wobbly hand-crank machine, flour absolutely everywhere, at least one strand thrown at the ceiling for science.
Braai. Not one dish, an entire afternoon. The fire does half the cooking and the arguments over the fire do the rest.
My mum's rainy-day sinigang, sour enough to make you wince. One spoonful and every cousin in the room is eight years old again.
Mansaf on the biggest tray we own, eaten standing, right hands only, elbow to elbow. The crowding is part of the recipe.

29.text: I smell the milk before pouring, even fresh from the shop. My mother grew up on a farm; I inherited her full suspicion of dairy.
Talking to plants. My father did it in the allotment every evening. Mine now receive a full weather report and occasional neighborhood gossip.
Checking the stove three times before leaving the house. My mother's worry, inherited whole, like the good china.
I cannot throw away jars. My grandmother kept hundreds through rationing. My cupboard is a museum of jam jars awaiting a crisis.
Reading the last page of a book first. My dad swore it was about deciding whether the journey deserved him. I finally get it now.
Saying 'text me when you land' to everyone, for any journey, including a walk to the corner shop. Thanks, Mum. I genuinely mean it.
Ironing handkerchiefs. Nobody uses them anymore. I iron them anyway, because the smell of the steam is my father on a Sunday morning.
Turning off lights in rooms people are actively using. My dad's electricity sermons live on in my hands. My own family is furious.
Salting the pasta water like the sea, no measuring, wrist only. My mother judged people who used spoons. I have become her. It's fine.
The silent treatment when I'm hurt. My father's habit, and the one thing of his I promised not to keep. Still working on it, honestly.
Keeping a little folded cash behind my phone case. My mother called it running money. Refugee habits skip nothing, not even a generation.
Whistling while doing dishes. My daughter now whistles the exact tuneless tune I stole from my dad. Three generations, zero melody between us.
I bow slightly on the phone. My father did it his whole working life in Osaka. The caller cannot see it. That was never the point.
Writing tiny pencil notes in book margins, arguing with the author. I once found my mum's copy of Jane Eyre — an entire feud in the margins.
Feeding anyone who enters the house, immediately, no exceptions. The plumber left with soup last Tuesday. My mother would be so proud.
Catastrophizing weather. One cloud and my father cancelled picnics. I now own four umbrellas and consult three forecast apps. They disagree.

31.text: Up at six before everyone, coffee alone on the balcony while the street sweepers work. Then family noise from eight onward, which I also love.
Wet market at seven, congee at nine, mahjong with the aunties by two, lose money to my mother by four, leftovers by seven. Perfect.
No alarm. Bakery run in pajamas, warm baguette eaten on the walk so it arrives home half gone. Long lunch. Nap. That's it, that's the day.
Church until noon with the singing loud, then my sister's place for rice and stew until the pot is scraped, then absolutely nothing until Monday.
Rain all day, mandatory. Blanket, tea, a fat novel, my cat mildly annoyed at my page-turning. Around five, someone else decides dinner.
Football on the dusty pitch at eight before the heat, sugarcane juice after, then sleeping through the afternoon with the fan on high.
Hour by hour? Nine, bike ride. Eleven, flea market, haggling badly. One, pierogi at grandma's. Three to six, unaccounted for. That gap is the perfect part.
The long call home. Two hours of my parents passing the phone around, camera aimed at foreheads and ceilings. My whole Sunday orbits around it.
Everyone home, nobody talking. Four people, four corners, four books, one pot of tea refilled without anyone asking. Peak family intimacy.
Pancakes with my kids while the kitchen gets destroyed, park until someone cries, naps in a pile, then pizza because I refuse to cook twice.
Start slow, ocean swim by ten even in winter, salt still in my hair through lunch, asleep on the couch by three with the cricket on. Bliss.
Cemetery first with fresh flowers for my husband, then coffee and cake with my sister, complaining about our knees for two hours. Lovely, truly.
Sleep till noon, obviously. Group chat breakfast review, gaming until my mum makes me walk the dog, which is secretly the best part of it.
Souq in the morning while it's cool, mint tea with my uncles until the political arguments get good, couscous at my grandmother's at two sharp.
A slow train somewhere green with my thermos and no fixed plan back. My wife thinks I go hiking. I mostly sit near cows, at peace.
Six loads of laundry, floors mopped, meals prepped, everything folded by dusk. My family calls it chores. Wrong. It is meditation with results.

33.text: The accent you are trying so hard to sand off will one day be the most interesting thing about you at every dinner party. Keep it.
Buy the guitar. The maths tutoring can survive one missed month. You'll remember none of the quadratics and all of the songs you didn't write.
That boy is not the love of your life. The girl laughing at your jokes in chemistry class, though — pay closer attention there.
Your father is scared, not angry. It took me thirty years to tell the difference. You could save us both the wait.
Learn grandma's recipes now, while her hands still remember. Write nothing down and you'll spend your forties guessing at the spices.
Nobody at school will remember the thing with the flagpole. You will not believe me. But I am telling you: nobody remembers.
Keep the diary. Yes, all of it, even the terrible poems. Your granddaughter will read it someday and finally understand you were a person.
The war ends. You grow old somewhere safe and boring, and boring turns out to be the greatest luxury ever invented.
Sunscreen. Every single day. I know it's cloudy in Manchester. This is not a joke. I am your face, calling from the future.
You do not have to earn rest. I know Ma says idle hands, but you'll burn out twice before forty learning what I could tell you right now.
Ask your grandfather about the ship. He will tell you everything if you simply ask, and you have three years left in which to do it. Ask.
Translating at every appointment for your parents isn't a burden, it's a superpower under construction. It becomes your entire career.
The plan fails. All of it. What replaces it is better than anything you currently have the imagination to want. Panic less.
Dance at the festivals. You skipped them to seem cool and mysterious. Nobody found you mysterious. They found you at home, sulking.
Say yes to the exchange year even though the phone call in another language terrifies you. That single year builds everything you love now.
Your mother's nagging about posture, savings, and vegetables? Correct. Every word of it. Enjoy being angry about that while you still can.

35.text: My grandmother microwaved the karaoke remote, mistaking it for leftovers. The smell lasted a week; the impressions of her face have lasted twenty years.
Dad drove us four hours to the ferry on the wrong Saturday. We camped in the car park anyway, and it's now our most beloved holiday story.
The Christmas the turkey slid off the platter and my aunt caught it against her cardigan like a rugby player. We ate it. Nobody discusses the cardigan.
My brother mailed our house keys to his pen pal in Finland along with the letter. We picnicked on the lawn for five hours awaiting my mother.
My uncle fell into the fish pond at a wedding reaching for the last spring roll. He rose from the water still holding it aloft, and ate it, dripping.
Mum texted 'your father and I are getting a divorce' to the family chat. She meant 'getting a Dyson'. Autocorrect. An aunt had already booked flights.
We buried a time capsule in 1999 with great ceremony. Dug it up in 2020: my father had forgotten to put anything inside. An empty biscuit tin, buried with speeches.
My grandfather washed his hearing aid with the dishes twice. The second time he blamed my grandmother for the wrong plate. They argued. He couldn't hear it.
Our goat ate the Eid guest list straight off the table. My mother greeted everyone at the door with total warmth and zero idea who had been invited.
Toddler me handed out my mum's honeymoon photos to dinner party guests like a tiny waiter with canapes. Tasteful ones, thankfully. Mostly.
My sister trained our parrot to say 'dinner's burnt' in my mother's exact voice. It chose the moment my in-laws first visited. It has never said it since.
The whole family followed the wrong hearse at my great-aunt's funeral. Two kilometres of solemn procession behind a stranger. She'd have laughed hardest.
Dad fixed the shower himself to save money. The plumber's exact words afterward: 'who declared war on this bathroom?' We framed the invoice.
In a rush, my mother swapped my school bag and my father's work bag. He opened a Hello Kitty pencil case at his big client meeting. Landed the client, allegedly.
Grandpa entered our cat in the village dog show out of spite after arguing with the organizer. The cat placed third of three entrants. He framed the ribbon.
New Year dumplings, and the lucky coin went missing. Found next morning in the teapot spout: my grandmother had hidden it out of habit. From her own game.

37.text: My parents' first meeting at the bus depot in 1974. She says he wore a terrible orange shirt; he insists it was mustard. One photo would settle fifty years of dispute.
My grandmother at my age, dancing. Everyone swears she was the best dancer in her village, yet every photo we have shows her sitting still, being respectable.
The kitchen of my childhood flat before demolition — the height marks on the doorframe, all six of us kids, in pencil only my mother could decode.
My father laughing. Really laughing, mouth open. He was serious in every photograph ever taken and unserious in half my memories of him.
All four of my grandparents in one room. They lived on three continents and never once met. My entire existence, and no photo to prove the collaboration.
Me asleep on my grandfather's back in the rice fields, which my aunts swear happened daily. I want evidence of ever being that safe.
The moment my brother, mid-argument that he could absolutely ride down the stairs, realized he could not. Airborne. Fully committed. The bike survived.
My mother the night before her wedding, when her sisters hennaed her hands and she laughed and cried at once. The one story all my aunts tell identically.
My great-grandfather's noodle stall in Guangzhou. It fed a whole street for thirty years and left not one image behind, just a wooden ladle we still use.
My wife across the library table the first moment I saw her, taken from my exact seat. I'd hang it facing my desk, so the view never changes.
My daughter's face the first second she ever saw snow. I was too busy watching to reach for my phone, which is maybe why I remember it perfectly.
Every woman in my family in one line, my daughter to her great-great-grandmother, born 1898. Same nose, they say. We missed the photo by two years.
My grandmother's garden at its peak, before the drought took it. She grew dahlias people crossed town to see and never once thought to photograph them.
The five of us squeezed onto one motorbike heading to the beach, 1989. Illegal, absurd, and the happiest transport arrangement of my childhood.
My son meeting my father. One died two months before the other arrived. I would take a blurry fake, honestly. Just the two of them in a single frame.
My mum at the London clubs in the eighties, wearing the outfits she describes in suspicious detail. She was cool once and demands we believe it on faith.

39.text: The bus driver waited while I ran, then pretended he hadn't seen me and was merely checking his mirrors. We both maintained the fiction. Lovely man.
My daughter called just to describe her lunch to me. Eight full minutes about a sandwich. I would happily have listened to eighty.
First mango of the season, eaten over the sink the way my father taught me, juice to the elbows. No plate has ever improved a mango.
My tomato plant, presumed dead all winter, produced one defiant flower. I informed my husband like it was a birth announcement.
The rain began the exact moment I stepped inside my door. Not one drop earlier. I felt personally escorted home by the weather for once.
A stranger's toddler waved at me on the metro like we were old colleagues. I waved back. Best meeting of my week: no agenda, adjourned at my stop.
Found my grandmother's handwriting on a recipe card tucked into a book I finally opened. Today she told me how much cinnamon. Present tense, somehow.
My teenage son hugged me first. Unprompted, with no request attached to the end of it. I have been insufferable about it all day.
The pigeon on my window ledge has accepted me. We had coffee, in the sense that I had coffee and he judged me. Routine is routine.
The corner shop man remembered both my usual order and my exam results. Fourteen million people in this city, and one of them was keeping track of me.
Clean sheets, and I shaved my legs. That combination outranks most holidays, and I will die on this hill, freshly laundered.
My grandson taught me to send voice notes. I sent eleven. He answered all eleven. Patience like that deserves a medal, or at least my flat someday.
Heard my mother's laugh come out of my own mouth on a work call. Startled myself. She's been gone three years and is apparently also right here.
The visa document queue moved quickly and the clerk said my Portuguese was improving. Small mercy, big day, and I ate a pastel de nata about it.
The sun came out during my cigarette break. I quit smoking years ago but kept the break, and today it was five minutes of standing in warmth doing nothing.
My little brother saved me the last dumpling and denied it meant anything. It meant everything. We don't discuss feelings; we allocate food.
